title: Phở Bar
bodyHtml:
Menus often use non-English names for dishes that originate from other countries, along with descriptions in English. For example, a Vietnamese take-out menu might list Gỏi Cuốn: Salad rolls. Below are the names and descriptions of twenty dishes from a Vietnamese take-out menu in arbitrary order. Identify the correct correspondences; write your answers in the Answer Sheets.

Also note that two of the below dishes come from a section with the following description:

Our Famous Vietnamese Noodle Soup. Choice of rice noodle “Phở” or yellow noodle “Mì” and your selected finest meat in an aromatic beef broth with scallions, onion, and cilantro. Soups are served with a plate of bean sprouts, fresh basil, sliced lime, jalapeno.

(A)Lotus Stem Salad.
(B)Vietnamese Crepe. A traditional mixture of shrimp and pork, bean sprouts and a delicate sauce folded into a rice powder pancake.
(C)Noodle Soup with shredded chicken.
(D)Wonton Soup. Shrimp, pork dumplings, lettuce, onion and scallions in chicken broth.
(E)Beef stew “Huế Style”. Spicy lemon grass beef noodle soup and shrimp.
(F)Scallions Pancake. Fried sweet flour with scallions.
(G)Vermicelli1 with seafood sautéed with lemon grass sauce.
(H)Vermicelli with crispy spring rolls.
(I)Roasted Quail.
(J)Filet of salmon or catfish steamed with ginger, scallions, and Chef’s special sauce.
(K)Vermicelli with choice of grilled meat.
(L)Beef sautéed in curry sauce.
(M)Vermicelli with a choice of grilled meat with crispy spring rolls.
(N)Vermicelli with shrimp, choice of grilled meat, and crispy spring rolls.
(O)Saigon Ravioli Fried or Steamed. Homemade dumplings filled with a mixture of chicken, pork, and vegetable. Served with ginger dipping sauce.
(P)Teriyaki with choice of meat.
(Q)Vietnamese salad. Choice of poached shrimp, chicken, or combination, with shredded carrots, cabbage, fresh mints, roasted peanuts, onions and homemade dressing.
(R)Crispy Spring Rolls. A savory mixture of ground pork, taro, carrots, onion, rice vermicelli, and mushroom wrapped in spring roll and fried golden brown.
(S)Vermicelli with grilled shrimp.
(T)Sautéed crispy yellow noodle.

1Vermicelli are long, slender noodles.

hints.text: Start with the easiest anchors: the dishes whose names contain a word you already recognise from English or from the boxed noodle-soup description, and the descriptions that are only two or three words long. Every dish matches exactly one description, so each anchor you fix removes one option from all the others.

Treat the Vietnamese names as strings of building blocks and compare names that share blocks. If two names differ by exactly one word, their English descriptions should differ by exactly one ingredient. Line up the families of names (the ones beginning with the same first word, the ones ending with the same last word) against the families of descriptions and let the length and structure of each name tell you how long its description should be.

Worked example on data that is not graded here: the introduction tells you Gỏi Cuốn means salad rolls, so Gỏi carries the idea of a salad or a fresh roll. That single block instantly narrows any name starting with Gỏi to the salad descriptions, and then a second word inside the name decides which salad it is. Do the same trick with the boxed paragraph, which hands you two more blocks for free.

explanationHtml:
What kind of puzzle is this?

You are not expected to know Vietnamese. The trick is that both lists are built out of repeating pieces. Vietnamese dish names are compounds: a noodle or protein word, then words for how it is cooked and what goes with it. The English descriptions repeat in exactly the same way. So instead of translating, you compare patterns: names that share a word should have descriptions that share an ingredient.

Step 1: use the free information

The introduction gives you one translation outright: Gỏi Cuốn = salad rolls, so Gỏi has to do with salad. The boxed paragraph gives two more: Phở is the rice noodle and Mì is the yellow noodle. And a few names contain words borrowed straight into or out of English and French: Soup, Salmon, Rôti (roasted), Cà Ry (curry).

That already settles several rows. Soup Hoành Thánh is the only name containing "Soup", and "Wonton Soup" is the only description that is a soup other than the two noodle soups. Chim Cút Rôti pairs with "Roasted Quail" because of Rôti. Bò Xào Cà Ry is the curry one.

Step 2: match the two noodle-soup dishes

The box says only two dishes come from the noodle-soup section, and only two descriptions are noodle soups: "Noodle Soup with shredded chicken" and "Beef stew 'Huế Style'". One of the two names literally contains the words Phở and Mì from the box, plus Gà; the other contains the place name Huế, which is printed inside one of the descriptions. Once you spot the place name, both rows fall out at once.

Step 3: build the Bún family

Six names begin with Bún, and six descriptions begin with "Vermicelli" (plus one more, Bún Xào Đo Biến, that has extra cooking words). So Bún = vermicelli. Now sort by length and shared blocks:

  • The shortest Bún names have the shortest vermicelli descriptions.
  • Chả Giò appears both on its own (a two-piece appetiser) and inside longer names; the appetiser description is "Crispy Spring Rolls", so Chả Giò = crispy spring rolls.
  • Thịt Nướng shows up in the names that mention grilled meat, and Tôm in the ones that mention shrimp (compare Gỏi Tôm, the shrimp salad).

Now the longest name in the family, Bún Tôm Thịt Nướng Chả Giò, has to be the description that lists three things: shrimp, grilled meat and spring rolls — and the word order even lines up. Its neighbour without Tôm loses exactly the shrimp.

Step 4: the leftovers

Xào turns up in Bò Xào Cà Ry (sautéed in curry), Mì Xào and Bún Xào Đo Biến, so Xào = sautéed. Since Mì is the yellow noodle, Mì Xào is the sautéed crispy yellow noodle, and the vermicelli-with-seafood dish takes the remaining sautéed description.

Bánh starts three names and means a cake or pancake-like item: one is the crepe, one the scallion pancake (Hành = scallions, also visible in the fried-flour description), and one the fried-or-steamed dumplings — that last name contains Chiên Hoặc Hấp, and Hoặc "or" also appears in the salmon-or-catfish and the shrimp-or-chicken names, confirming the reading. Hấp reappears in the steamed fish name.

What remains are the two Gỏi salads: the one naming shrimp or chicken matches the long Vietnamese-salad description with poached shrimp or chicken, and the other one, Ngo Sen, matches "Lotus Stem Salad". Finally Thịt Lụi takes the only description left, "Teriyaki with choice of meat" — and Thịt "meat" is exactly the block you already met in Thịt Nướng.

The moral

Cross-checking beats guessing. Each time you fix a pair, cross it off both lists; the process-of-elimination pressure at the end is what makes the last few rows easy.

Vietnamese diacritics transcribed exactly as printed, including B5 'Bún Xào Đo Biến' and B8 'Gỏi Ngo Sen', which look like menu typos but are left as printed. Choices are the 20 option letters A-T, since the answer sheet asks for a letter.
